question: In many regions of Greece, especially in island, mountainous and remote areas, the lack of stable public funding, the chronic understaffing of the National Health System and the unbalanced geographical distribution of medical resources create conditions of health exclusion.

Citizens of these regions often lack timely access to specialist doctors, diagnostic tests or treatments and are forced to travel hundreds of kilometres or go to urban centres, at significant financial and psychological cost. According to recent Eurostat data,1 21.9 % of Greeks stated that they did not receive medical care due to cost, distance or long waits, the highest rate in the EU.

The most vulnerable groups and isolated areas are disproportionately affected.2 While for 2023, Greece was in last place in terms of breast cancer screening, with a rate of only 14.5 %,3 presenting the greatest deviation in the implementation of the European plan to combat cancer and the EU cohesion policy, which seek equal opportunities in prevention and treatment.4 In view of the above: 1.
How will the Commission ensure the implementation of the European plan to combat cancer in remote and island areas of Greece?
What measures will the Commission take to reduce economic and territorial inequalities in access to specialist health services?
Does the Commission intend to increase funding for public health infrastructure, with an emphasis on cancer care and screening?

title=Cancer_screening_statistics. Breast cancer is the most common form of cancer in women and one of the most deadly in the EU. Screening contributes significantly to reducing mortality, through early diagnosis, less invasive treatments and cure rates that exceed 95 % in the early stages of the disease.
However, despite the importance of early detection as a survival factor, significant inequalities and barriers to access to screening persist.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.12.

2025) In full respect of the Member States’ responsibility for organising and delivering health services1 including prioritising public health infrastructure projects on cancer care and screening, Cohesion Policy and the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) funding support Member States in improving equal access to healthcare and strengthening the resilience of health systems. EU-wide, EUR 7.

3 billion from the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) and Interreg, and some EUR 3.8 billion from the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+)2, as well as about EUR 42 billion from the RRF, are channelled to health-related investments, including measures to enhance access to specialist healthcare services3.

For the 2021-2027 period, Greece has earmarked EUR 362 million from the ERDF and EUR 250 million from the ESF+ in public funding for investments aimed at improving the accessibility and effectiveness of its healthcare services including the purchase of state-ofthe-art medical equipment.

The EU supports health reforms and investments under the Greek recovery and resilience plan, such as the renovation of 156 primary healthcare units and 80 hospitals, the creation of 312 chronic disease management units across the country, as well as the ‘Implementation of the National Public Health Prevention Program Spiros Doxiadis’, providing breast, cervical and colorectal cancer screening as well as cardiovascular disease screening to the Greek population4.

Finally, the EU provides funding to support cancer care and screening, under Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan, through the EU4Health Programme. The Joint Action EUCanScreen5, with EUR 31 million, also serves to support the implementation of the 2022 Council Recommendation on cancer screening67.
